clue.text: Looks at geese

definitions.meaning: to take a gander is to have a look, so the verb in the third person means looks at
the clue uses the plural loosely for male birds

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: 'gander' as slang for a glance gives the verb, and a gander is a male goose.

clue.text: Better call him by another name!

definitions.text: Better call him by another name!

parts.words: Better call him by another name!
parts.note: reads as advice to rename someone, but it asks for another word for a better, one who places bets

explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' looks like 'preferably' but is a noun: someone who bets.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a person who bets is a punter or wagerer.

clue.text: Reports chap wants from him

parts.note: reads as someone demanding accounts from a man, but describes the person from whom stories are expected

explanation.walkthrough: The clue also splits into NEWS for 'Reports' and MAN for 'chap'.
explanation.definitionFit: A journalist is the one an editor or reader expects to supply reports.

clue.text: Spa found, travelling via outskirts of eindhoven

indicators.note: travelling means the letters of via and the pair are on the move into a new order
outskirts of means the first and last letters of eindhoven

explanation.surface: A spa town discovered on a journey that passes the edge of a Dutch city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outskirts of eindhoven' gives EN, its first and last letters; 'travelling' rearranges VIA plus EN. Eindhoven is a Dutch city.
explanation.definitionFit: Evian-les-Bains is a French spa town on Lake Geneva, famous for its mineral water.

clue.text: Unable to see tourist attractions in the French quarter

indicators.note: in means the French article and the quarter go inside the word for attractions

parts.note: the sights are what tourists go to see
le is French for the
S, south, is one of the four quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: A blind visitor to the sights of the French Quarter of New Orleans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal. 'French quarter' looks like the New Orleans district, but it splits into the French article and a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: Sightless means blind, lacking vision.

clue.text: Hang the expense in America!

indicators.note: 'in' puts one piece inside the other

parts.note: a spend is an informal noun for an outlay or expense

explanation.surface: An exclamation of extravagance, 'Hang the expense!', said by someone in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface borrows the idiom 'hang the expense'; in the wordplay 'Hang' is the definition and the expense is placed after America.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspend something is to hang it from above, as a lamp from a ceiling.

clue.text: Economised on the day, but unhappy about it

indicators.note: about means the word for unhappy goes round the day

parts.note: sad means unhappy
VE Day, 8 May 1945, marked Victory in Europe

explanation.surface: Someone scrimped on the big day and felt miserable about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is the container signal; the day is Victory in Europe Day, 8 May 1945. 'on the' and 'but ... it' are only links.
explanation.definitionFit: To save is to economise, to spend less and put money by.

clue.text: Erudite student has left over a year

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the left letter sits above the year

parts.note: a scholar is a student or learner

explanation.surface: A learned undergraduate who has outstayed his course by a year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reads as more than a year, but in a down answer it places L above Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Scholarly means learned, showing deep academic knowledge.

clue.text: Fetter made to measure for china conflict

parts.note: an en is a printer's unit of measure

indicators.note: conflict means the letters of china are at odds and fall into a new order

explanation.surface: Bespoke chains made for a war in China.
explanation.walkthrough: EN is the printer's measure; 'conflict' rearranges CHINA. 'made to' and 'for' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: To enchain is to bind in chains, just as to fetter is to shackle.

clue.text: One has this time to pay

definitions.text: One has this time to pay

parts.words: One has this time to pay
parts.note: reads as a general remark about paying, but describes the day by which a bill must be settled

explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description of the deadline on an invoice, the day payment falls owing.

clue.text: Crying out, like gull catching fish

parts.note: a mew is a seagull, especially the common gull
a ling is a long-bodied sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A noisy gull squawks as it seizes a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' and 'catching' only join the pieces: the gull comes first and the fish follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Mewling is feeble whimpering or crying, like an infant's or a kitten's.

clue.text: Car for Clive — he ordered it

indicators.note: ordered means the letters of Clive and he are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Clive's new car was bought because he ordered it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' reads as placing an order for the car, but it signals that CLIVE and HE are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A car is one kind of vehicle, a means of road transport.

clue.text: Plated in tin, a medal is cast

indicators.note: a casting reshapes metal, so is cast tells us to rework the letters of tin and a medal

explanation.surface: A medal produced by casting in tin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is cast' signals the anagram of TIN plus A MEDAL; 'in' is only a link after the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Laminated means covered with a thin layer or sheet, as metal plating overlays a surface.

clue.text: In Bali, an abundant plant

indicators.note: In tells us the letters sit inside the run of words Bali, an abundant

explanation.surface: A plant that grows profusely on the Indonesian island of Bali.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a place for the plant but signals a run of letters inside 'Bali, an abundant'.
explanation.definitionFit: A liana is a woody climbing vine of tropical forests.

clue.text: From cattle station, sprinted to church

parts.note: sprinted means ran fast

explanation.surface: Someone races away from a cattle farm to get to church.
explanation.definitionFit: A ranch is a large farm for raising livestock, which Australians call a cattle station.

clue.text: Almost lift one head, despite weight

indicators.note: almost means the word for lift stops short of its final letter

parts.note: to heave is to lift with effort
I is the Roman numeral for one
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Sheerness

explanation.surface: Struggling to raise one's head despite being weighed down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts HEAVE to HEAV; a ness is a headland, as in the place names Sheerness and Dungeness.
explanation.definitionFit: Heaviness is the quality of having great weight.

clue.text: Anne cured by doctoring and patience

indicators.note: doctoring means tampering with, so the letters of Anne cured are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: Anne was cured by a doctor's care and her own patience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doctoring' reads as medical treatment but signals the anagram of ANNE CURED; 'by' and 'and' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Endurance is the capacity to put up with hardship calmly, much as patience is.

clue.text: How did a central position leave one set apart?

indicators.note: central means the word for position sits in the middle of did

parts.note: a stance is a position or posture

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about how being in the middle can leave someone isolated.
explanation.walkthrough: The question 'How did...?' is answered by DID with STANCE at its centre; 'leave one' joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To distance is to place far off, so distanced means kept separate.

clue.text: Cracks and creases needing vacuous valets' adjustments

indicators.note: adjustments means the letters of creases and the extra pair are rearranged
vacuous means empty, so valets' loses its insides and leaves its outer letters

explanation.surface: Valets with nothing in their heads are needed to iron out wrinkles in clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vacuous valets' gives VS, the first and last letters of VALETS; 'adjustments' then rearranges CREASES plus VS.
explanation.definitionFit: Crevasses are deep fissures or splits in a glacier's ice.

clue.text: Raucous laughs heard during hen-party?

definitions.meaning: literally a gathering of hens, which make clucking noises

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: shrill harsh laughter, and the clucking noise hens make.

clue.text: Ended when former partner pried outrageously

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner

indicators.note: outrageously means the letters of pried behave wildly and rearrange

explanation.surface: A relationship finished when the ex snooped too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outrageously' signals the anagram of the fodder 'pried', giving PIRED; 'when' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Expired means came to an end, as a contract or licence does.

clue.text: Called wipers by soldiers in France

definitions.text: Called wipers by soldiers in France

parts.words: Called wipers by soldiers in France
parts.note: British troops on the Western Front in the First World War anglicised the name of a Flemish town as Wipers

explanation.walkthrough: The town is in Belgium, but it lay on the front the British army knew as 'France'; the troops' nickname mangled its pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the Belgian town besieged in the First World War, mispronounced by British soldiers as Wipers.

clue.text: Rejecting the German factory-worker's display of Ulster arms

indicators.note: rejecting means the German article is thrown back and read in reverse

parts.note: der is German for the
a hand is a manual worker in a factory or on a farm

explanation.surface: A factory hand turns down a German emblem in favour of the Ulster coat of arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejecting' turns DER to RED. Ulster is the northern province of Ireland; its heraldic emblem is an open red hand.
explanation.definitionFit: The heraldic emblem of the Irish province of Ulster is an open crimson palm.

clue.text: Drinkers also having meals

definitions.meaning: to sup is to drink, so those who sup are drinkers

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: people who sip a drink, and evening repasts.

clue.text: Island around jail from which son escaped

parts.note: around gives CA

indicators.note: escaped means the son has got out, so it is removed from the word for jail

parts.note: a prison is a jail
taken as written

explanation.surface: An island surrounds a jail from which a young man has broken out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'escaped' takes SON out of PRISON, leaving PRI; 'from which' only links it to the jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Capri is an island in the Bay of Naples off southern Italy.

clue.text: When praised, went to pieces

definitions.meaning: to crack something up is to praise it highly
to crack up is to have a breakdown, to lose composure

explanation.definitionFit: Two idioms: talked up or extolled, and suffered a nervous collapse.

clue.text: Suitable containers?

parts.note: read as 'suit-able', containers able to hold suits, luggage for clothes

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark asks you to split 'Suitable' into suit plus able, pointing to suitcases.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: boxes or luggage that hold a suit of clothes.

clue.text: Shrimp that whales have a right to kill

indicators.note: to here means the right letter is added in to the word kill

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A protest over whether whales may kill shrimps.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes into KILL after its first letter. Krill are the tiny crustaceans that baleen whales feed on.
explanation.definitionFit: Krill are small shrimplike crustaceans eaten in vast numbers by whales.

clue.text: Generosity shown aboard big ship

parts.note: big means large
SS, for steamship, is a standard abbreviation for a ship

explanation.surface: Lavish giving is on display on board a large vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Largess is liberal giving of gifts or money, a spirit of open-handedness.

clue.text: Atmosphere in clubs when I'm late getting in

parts.note: C is the card-playing abbreviation for clubs

indicators.note: getting in means the letters of I'm go inside the word late

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Arriving late at the nightclubs to find the mood of the place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting in' makes LIMATE, the inner piece placed within 'late'. 'when' and 'in' are only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Climate is the prevailing mood or feeling, as in a climate of fear.

clue.text: Cruel people giving one hell on Saturdays

indicators.note: on is read as set on to or in, so the word for hell is placed within the Saturdays

parts.note: Sat is the abbreviation for Saturday, so Saturdays gives SATS
Dis is one name for hell, the underworld city in Dante and the Roman god of the dead

explanation.surface: People who make others suffer at the weekend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is the container signal; 'giving' is only a link. Dis is the Roman god of the underworld and Dante's city of hell, hence 'one hell'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sadists take pleasure in inflicting pain on others, the very picture of cruelty.

clue.text: Fools — amateur cowboys the Spanish take in

indicators.note: take in means the word for amateur cowboys holds the Spanish article inside

parts.note: dudes are city folk playing at being cowboys, as on a dude ranch
el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Inexperienced cowhands are fooled by Spanish tricksters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take in' looks like deceive, echoing the definition, but here it is the container signal. Dude ranches cater for city visitors playing cowboy.
explanation.definitionFit: To delude someone is to deceive or mislead them, making a fool of them.
